prerequisites: Minimal computer skills in Windows interface, file management, and local/internet network access.
Availability of a personal computer at home for individual work.
Ability to integrate with other students in work groups for collective tasks.

learning_outcomes.text: Students must be able to gather and interpret relevant data (normally within their area of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific or ethical issues.

Students must have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in an area of study that builds on general secondary education, and is usually at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes aspects implying knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.
Students must have developed those learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

Students must know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competences usually demonstrated through the elaboration and defense of arguments and problem-solving within their area of study.
Knowledge and skills to apply graphic engineering techniques.
Ability to apply new technologies, including information and communication technologies.
Ability to manage information, handle and apply technical specifications and necessary legislation for engineering practice.
Basic knowledge of production and manufacturing systems.
Spatial vision ability and knowledge of graphic representation techniques, both by traditional methods of metric and descriptive geometry, and through computer-aided design applications.
Basic knowledge about the use and programming of computers, operating systems, databases and software with application in engineering.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to Interpolation. Concept of interpolation. Unisolvence.
Polynomial interpolation in one variable. Lagrangian interpolation: Indeterminate coefficients, Newton's idea, Divided differences, Lagrange's idea. Taylor interpolation. Hermite interpolation.
Construction of interpolating polynomial parametric curves. Parameter selection.
Convergence problems in polynomial interpolation. Weierstrass and Faber theorems.
Spline functions. Degree and class. Spline interpolation. Examples. Basis of spline functions.
Interpolation in two variables. Unisolvent problems in Pn and Qn,m. Introduction to spline interpolation in two variables. Construction of Lagrange functions.
Approximation. Concept of approximation. Quantitative approximation: Least squares. Qualitative approximation: Bernstein polynomials. Shape preservation.
B-splines.
Approximation of one-variable functions.
Approximation of curves. Bezier curves. B-spline curves. NURBS curves.
Approximation of two-variable functions. Approximation of surfaces. Bezier, B-spline and NURBS surfaces.
Parametric variational 3D CAD systems. Creation of parts and assemblies.
Spatial wireframe models. Spatial geometry in CAD environments.
Planar curves. Spatial curves. Bezier and B-Spline curves.
Planar surfaces. Polygonal faces. Manipulation of planar surfaces.
Warped surfaces: ruled, swept, revolved, curve-bounded, lofted. Manipulation of warped surfaces.
Generalized three-dimensional meshes.
Modeling of industrial products composed of surfaces.
Preparation of drawings from surface-based three-dimensional designs.
Applications I: Discretization of volumes for analysis using the Finite Element Technique.
Applications II: Simulation of a part's stress behavior under external loads.
Applications III: Optimization of a part's design based on stress behavior analysis.
Applications IV: Obtaining machining trajectories for complex surfaces for manufacturing on Numerical Control machines.
Applications V: Photorealistic representations. Texturing and lighting techniques. Creation of videos of virtual 3D environments.
Practice: Preliminaries. Mathematica and plotting curves and surfaces with this software.
Practice: Representing curves using polynomial interpolation of one-variable functions.
Practice: Representing curves using polynomial interpolation of parametric curves.
Practice: Representing curves using Spline interpolation.
Practice: Representing surfaces using polynomial and Spline interpolation.
Practice: Representing curves using least squares approximation and Bernstein polynomials.
Practice: Representing surfaces using Bezier surface approximation.
Practice: Representing curves using B-Spline curve approximation.
Practice: Representing surfaces using B-Spline surface approximation.
Practice: Representing curves using rational Bezier curve approximation.
Practice: Representing curves using Nurbs curve approximation.
Practice: Representing surfaces using rational Bezier surface approximation.
Practice: Representing surfaces using Nurbs surface approximation.
Practice: Explanation of the final project.
Practice: Sketching (1/2).
Practice: Sketching (2/2): Creation of 2D sketches and drawings necessary for 3D part generation (solid) and profile structures (surfaces).
Practice: Part (1/3).
Practice: Part (2/3).
Practice: Part (3/3): Options for "solid type" 3D modeling of industrial parts.
Practice: Surfaces (1/3).
Practice: Surfaces (2/3).
Practice: Surfaces (3/3): Options for "surface type" 3D modeling of industrial parts.
Practice: Drawing (1/2).
Practice: Drawing (2/2): Options for drawing 2D planes and obtaining normalized projections (views) from a 3D part.
Practice: Assemblies (1/1): For an industrial mechanism, obtaining its 3D model assembled in its operating position, normalized views, and assembly drawing (exploded perspective).
Practice: Simulation (1/2): Analysis, using CAE software, of the stress behavior of a part under external loads.
Practice: Simulation (2/2): Optimization of the geometry and dimensions of an industrial part with CAE stress analysis software.
Practice: Group Project (1/1): Presentation and defense of the group project.
teaching_methods: Expository classes (lectures) in large groups, covering theoretical content, general examples, and introductory activities.
Small group classes (computer labs) for problem solving, practical activities, seminars, and debates.
Weekly practical sessions, with theoretical introductions by the professor and resolution of exercises, sometimes completed in class or at home.
Individual final project, chosen by the student, covering course content and presented in class.
Group project (maximum two students), with choice of thematic, delivered electronically, presented, and defended.
assessment_rules: The grading system follows RD 1125/2003. Contents of Block 1 and Block 2 are evaluated separately, each contributing 50% to the final grade. For Block 1, students have the option to choose between an individual project or a theory exam, which accounts for 50% of the block's grade. Grades for Block 1 (Active Participation) and Block 2 (Practices) are maintained for ordinary and extraordinary calls. For the extraordinary call, students may request to be evaluated solely by the Block 2 Practical Exam, which would then account for 100% of the final grade.
